The spread is not mysterious: a learn that FAILS spends its whole budget, so a pass costs what its failures cost and which rows fail varies. A channel that alarms on a third of runs is the one that gets `|| true`d, taking the inviolable channel dark with it (R3.9/CLI-1). FIXED by recording the MAXIMUM observed rather than the mean -- which asks the question actually worth asking, "did spend blow past anything we have ever seen", and still fails a 2.5x blow-up (verified). `cost_per_rep` rides along so the mean stays recoverable: the expected cost and the alarm threshold are different questions and the artifact must not force one to stand in for the other.

**WHAT CI RUNS WAS A HAND-TYPED LIST IN CI, AND NOTHING COULD FAIL FOR AN OMISSION -- TWICE, IN THE SAME FILE.** (a) The six mutation registries were six hand-typed `prove_red.py <registry> --tests ...` steps in `ci.yml`, and the killer suite rode on the command line. A seventh registry added under `tests/mutations/` and not added there would simply never have run, with every job green and no test in the suite able to fail for it -- the "quiet is an allowlist" defect (R3.9/CLI-1) wearing a CI hat, which this project has now shipped twice (`flow run-all`'s third status bucket; a test in no shard). The killer suite living in the workflow was the second half of the same thing: invisible to whoever wrote or reviewed the registry, and structurally unable to say that mutant 3 is killed by one file and mutant 7 by another. (b) `tests/test_ci_provisioning.py` read `ci.yml` ALONE. That was not a simplification but an unstated assumption that there would only ever be one workflow file, and it was LATENT until 0.6 added the second -- which installs a browser and runs on a schedule, i.e. is precisely that file's subject, and would have been entirely unscanned by the budget pin, the apt pin and the byte-identical-install pin. **FIXED by deriving both sets**: the registry set comes from the directory (`mutation_sweep.registries`), each registry declares its own `KILLED_BY` with a per-mutant override, the workflow set comes from `.github/workflows/*.y*ml`, and the TIER SPLIT -- which registries the merge gate may run and which need the weekly job's Chromium -- is read out of the tier manifest rather than declared, because `red-proof` installs no Playwright deliberately and a killer-suite leg with a browser cell fails EVERY mutant's baseline (8 failed / 135 passed on both CI arms, green locally). Both directions are asserted: a registry named in a workflow `run:` fails, a workflow file contributing no step fails, and the weekly job growing `--tier fast` fails -- that last one because it would leave the nine known mutants swept by NEITHER job.

**THE GENERIC-OPERATOR HALF OF 0.6 IS MEASURED AND BLOCKED, AND THE CHEAP DESIGN IS WRONG RATHER THAN MERELY EXPENSIVE.** reshape-plan 0.6 asks for "generic operators on a frozen hot-file list ... a survivor not in `known_survivors` fails". Sized by AST over the six hot files (`flow.py`, `flows.py`, `locators.py`, `safety.py`, `cache.py`, `recorder.py`): **2848 mutants** -- 1076 `if`->True/False, 459 bool-constant flips, 416 int +-1, 328 and/or swaps, 145 `not` drops, 302 comparison flips, 2 `while`->False. Against the fast tier, the only killer broad enough for most of them, that is **70.4 h serial**; a GitHub job is capped at 6 h, so even four-way sharding leaves 17.6 h a shard. **BUT THE RUNTIME IS THE LESSER PROBLEM.** Against a NARROW killer it is cheap (3.6 h) and actively misleading: the `if` family on `safety.py` -- the best case in the repository, 310 lines, no browser within reach, two test files aimed at it -- gives 16 mutants, **6 survivors (38%)**, and **all six are killed by the fast tier** (measured, one at a time). Extrapolated, the cheap design would report on the order of a THOUSAND holes that are not holes, each needing a hand-typed `KNOWN_SURVIVORS` reason -- the transcription class this register keeps ending, feeding a loud channel nobody can discharge, which is how a channel gets switched off wholesale (R3.9/CLI-1). **SO THE MISSING COMPONENT IS NOT MORE MUTANTS: IT IS A COVERAGE-DERIVED KILLER SELECTION** -- run only the tests that actually execute the mutated line, which is what every real mutation tool does, and which makes the killer right BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by somebody's guess. That is its own instrument (a per-line coverage map, regenerated as the tree changes, with the same fixed-point and staleness problems the tier manifest has) and it is not this slice. **A NEAR-MISS WORTH KEEPING:** `if slot_values:` -> False in `safety.idempotency_key` reads as a live inviolable-#3 defect -- two rows of a parameterized write would mint the SAME key and a backend dedupe would silently drop rows 2..N -- and it is fully guarded; seven fast cells in `tests/test_slots.py` reach it. A survivor against a killer you chose is a statement about your choice. The curated half of 0.6 shipped: 75 mutants across seven registries, weekly, on a derived list.

**"CI HAS NO DOCKER DAEMON" IS ASSERTED IN TWO MODULES AND ITS EVIDENCE DOES NOT SAY THAT.** `benchmarks/oracle_liveness.py`'s docstring says Docker is "present on a developer host and absent on CI", and `CLAUDE.md` carries it as the third axis of local-vs-CI divergence. Traced to its source, the claim rests on 0.121.0: two cells reached `await_ready()` for real and failed BOTH CI arms with `NOT WRITABLE` while passing here against a live Gitea. **That is a container which is not RUNNING**, which is trivially true of a job that never started one — it is not an observation about the daemon. The two readings have completely different consequences: if there is no daemon, reshape-plan 2.4's weekly benchmark needs a self-hosted runner; if there is, it is an ordinary job. This is the same ambiguity class that put a wrong prerequisite into `reshape-plan.md` section 13 one day after section 13 was written to prevent it (a CI `cancelled` meaning three different things), and it was corrected there by MEASURING rather than by re-reading. **MEASURED HERE THE SAME WAY**: `benchmarks/substrate_check.py` prints the daemon's version before it attempts anything, and the `substrates` job runs it on every pull request that touches the bench. Whatever the answer, the guard in `tests/test_substrates.py` stays — it closes a real leak (a unit test reaching a LIVE substrate on the developer's machine and passing for the wrong reason) and that hazard is independent of what CI has. The finding stays open until the two docstrings are corrected to say what was actually observed. **MEASURED AND REFUTED, 2026-08-26.** The `substrates` job ran on a GitHub-hosted ubuntu runner and reported `{"docker_on_path": true, "version": "28.0.4", "compose": "2.38.2"}`, then brought Gitea up in **12.5 s**, reached writable at 12.6 s and seeded in **8.7 s**. So CI has a daemon, 2.4's weekly benchmark is an ordinary job, and no self-hosted runner is needed. **THE GUARD WAS RIGHT AND ITS STATED REASON WAS WRONG**, which is the part worth keeping: the real asymmetry is one level in -- a developer host runs a LIVE, SEEDED substrate between sessions and a CI job starts with nothing running, so a cell that reaches Docker still passes here against a real Gitea and still fails both CI arms. `tests/test_substrates.py`'s autouse fixture is unchanged; only its message is. Corrected in all three places that carried the claim (`benchmarks/oracle_liveness.py`, that fixture, and `CLAUDE.md`'s third axis).

**THE WEEKLY BENCHMARK'S FIRST REAL RUN FAILED BECAUSE THE JOB ASSUMED A PROVISIONED SUBSTRATE -- WHICH IS R4.109's ASYMMETRY, ONE LAYER DOWN, IN THE SLICE THAT CORRECTED IT.** 2.4a shipped a `customer-bench` job with `needs: substrates`. **`needs:` is ORDERING, NOT A SHARED MACHINE**: every GitHub job gets a fresh runner, so the containers the `substrates` job started did not exist in the job that pays. And `score_one` calls `substrate.reset()` and `await_ready()` but never `up()`, because on a developer host the substrate is already running between sessions. **Measured, run 33023685942**: all seven Gitea scenarios raised `SubstrateError: no seed at /data/gitea/seed.db -- call snapshot() once after seeding`, and the run cost nothing because nothing got as far as an LLM call. **A SECOND GAP BEHIND THE FIRST**: `seed()` does NOT take the snapshot `reset()` restores from, and nothing in `benchmarks/` ever called `snapshot()` -- on a developer host somebody ran it by hand once and the world persisted. So bringing the substrate up would not have been enough either. **THREE GUARDS BEHAVED CORRECTLY AND ARE WHY THIS COST $0.00**: the seed precondition named its own remedy (a guard added in an earlier slice for exactly this), every scenario was attributed to the HARNESS family rather than scored as a product failure (R4.99), and `build_bench_record` REFUSED to publish a record over an all-unscored corpus rather than rendering the mean of an empty list as 0.0. The safety net worked; the defect was purely the workflow wiring. **FIXED** by provisioning inside the paying job (`substrate_check --substrate gitea --keep`) and by making `check()` snapshot whenever it seeds -- not behind a flag, because a `--no-snapshot` would be a way to build the broken thing on purpose and no caller wants one. **VERIFIED against the real condition** rather than reasoned: the local Gitea volume was WIPED to reproduce a fresh runner, provisioned from nothing (up 12.3 s, seed 25.8 s), and `reset()` -- the call that raised on CI -- then succeeded. `tests/test_substrate_check.py` pins the class both ways: a job running a scored corpus must provision in the SAME job, and its provisioning step must carry `--keep` (a step without it tears the substrate down before the corpus reaches it, which is the same failure from the side a reader would least expect). Both are armed against the shape that actually shipped.

**ODOO'S CHEAP ROUTE IS CLOSED: D6 IS REFUTED BY ITS OWN MANDATED MEASUREMENT, AND THE GATE IS CORRECT AT EVERY BRANCH.** D6 proposed routing a wire-promoted step to the PRECISE form-scope gate instead of the whole-page one, and made itself conditional on measuring the action types first. Measured at 0.139.0, **$0.4634 across four Odoo learns**: 10 wire-promoted steps across the three scenarios that actually refused: **6 `navigate`** (no locator, no scope -- the precise gate is STRUCTURALLY unreachable, there is no element to scope) and **4 `click`** (scope AND locator -- the precise gate ALREADY, and it refused anyway). **BOTH BRANCHES REFUSE, FOR DIFFERENT REASONS**: `odoo-menu-nav` with `mutation gate: page drift` (the fallback), `odoo-sort-list` with `mutation gate: target missing/ambiguous` -- the PRECISE branch's own first failure mode, so the gate D6 wanted to route steps to was ALREADY judging them and refused anyway. That failure is `resolve(..., unique=True)` unable to bind uniquely on a generated DOM: a LOCATOR problem, not a scope problem, and `unique=True` is a deliberate write-safety choice that is correct for anything believed to be a write. **THE CHAIN IS: R4.27 marks an Odoo read as a write -> the write-safety machinery correctly refuses on ambiguity or drift -> an ordinary read becomes a hard refusal.** Nothing in the gate is wrong; the marking is. Narrowing it would weaken write safety for steps the system believes are writes, which is what D0 was blocked for. **WHAT THIS IS NOT: a claim that the product gets Odoo WRONG.** In three reps plus four measurement runs no Odoo scenario produced `wrong_data`; `mode="auto"` falls through to a re-author and the answer still arrives. What is lost is the 0-LLM deterministic replay -- the product's central claim -- so on this class of app it degrades to an ordinary LLM agent. **THE CLASS, NOT THE APP**: `is_write_request` keys on the HTTP METHOD, so this is every app that serves reads over POST (GraphQL SPAs, JSON-RPC), which is where R4.27's original 12/12 was measured -- not on Odoo at all. **A SIGNAL, NOT YET A FINDING**: `odoo-sort-list`'s gate refusal is itself a locator failure, so R4.27 may be partly masking a second independent Odoo problem (locator ambiguity on generated markup) and fixing R4.27 alone might not unblock 2.4b. One message is not a measurement. **THE MEASUREMENT CORRECTED ITSELF TWICE** -- from scenario one the conclusion was "the precise gate is structurally unreachable", which is false of 40% of the population; scenario two produced no gated step. The plan budgeted ~$0.10 for ONE run, and one run would have shipped a wrong `src/` change to the write rail. Reproduce with `python -m benchmarks.gate_probe <cache>`, which ships with the refutation.

**R4.27 SETS THE RATE OF R4.84's EXPOSURE, AND NOTHING RECORDS THE INTERACTION.** Filed on the survey's recommendation, and it is worth filing whatever is decided about R4.27 itself. R4.84 records that three doors (`cli_root`, `daemon_run`, `run_many`) can reach a full re-author with NO flow-level gates, and re-authoring a write flow PERFORMS THE WRITE AGAIN. Separately, R4.27's misfiling makes the mutation gate refuse 58% of Odoo replays, and `mode="auto"` falls through to a re-author on an irrecoverable replay failure. **So the over-marking MULTIPLIES traffic through the ungated re-author door — on exactly the app class where reads and writes share a wire shape and are therefore hardest to tell apart if one of them is real.** Neither finding is wrong on its own and neither names the other. The interaction means the status-quo option (accept the limitation) is NOT safety-neutral in the second order, which is how it was being described. Not a new mechanism and not a new door — a rate, on an existing one, that nobody was accounting for.

**THREE PIECES OF PROSE OUTLIVED THE THING THEY DESCRIBED, one of them operator-facing and self-contradicting.** Found while surveying R4.27. (a) `_auth_retry_allowed`'s refusal told the operator to run `flow inspect` and then said "the mark can come from the wire or from the step's wording; which of the two it was is not recorded" — FALSE since 0.92.0, and `cli.py`'s inspect renderer prints exactly that provenance three lines of code away. The message sent a reader to the one command that answers the question, to tell them it had no answer. (b) `run_all`'s undeclared-write refusal said "visibility is the whole of the remedy until a `mutating` mark can say WHY it was set" — it can, since the same release. (c) `CLAUDE.md` cited `docs/parked/README.md` for the parked 0.76.0 attribution branch; that path is not on `main` (it lives on `feat/shared-causal-attribution`), so the one pointer into the most expensive parked history in this register resolved to nothing. **FIXED**: both messages now name the provenance and what to do with it, and the CLAUDE.md pointer names the branch. The auth-retry text is pinned by `tests/goldens/auth_retry_truth.json`, so the change is a reviewed golden diff — every `retry` boolean is unchanged and only the message moved, which is the direction that golden exists to make checkable.

**LOCATOR AMBIGUITY, NOT R4.27, IS WHAT BLOCKS ODOO — MEASURED, AND IT REVERSES THE WORKING ASSUMPTION.** R4.111's tail recorded a signal: one mutation-gate refusal was itself `target missing/ambiguous`, a locator failure wearing a gate's message. It is now a measurement. **#1, the A/B**: the same recipe replayed twice against the same substrate, differing only in whether the `wire` marks are set. Control -- step 1 `click`, `mutating: True`, `gate: drift`, `gate_bound_by: none`, "mutation gate: target missing/ambiguous". Demoted -- same step, no mark, no gate, `bound_by: none`, "locator unresolved or ambiguous (drift)". **`bound_by: none` in BOTH arms**: the locator never resolved either way, and the gate was reporting a locator failure it reached first. Run TWICE -- on a day-old recipe and on one learned minutes earlier -- so staleness is excluded. Demotion's only real effect was restoring the auth-refresh retry, which then failed identically. `odoo-menu-nav` is worse for the thesis: both arms fail at step 0, an UNMARKED navigate, so R4.27 is irrelevant to it. **#2, the census** over the three-rep series' 18 non-passing rows: 6 no-replay (the learn produced nothing), 6 gate page/form drift, **4 locator failures with no gate involved at all**, 1 gate target-missing (itself a locator failure), 1 data-not-found. So four rows show the locator problem with no mark in the picture, and #1 shows the gated rows convert into it. **CONSEQUENCE: R4.27 is a real correctness defect and NOT the Odoo blocker**; 2.4b must not be costed as "fix R4.27, get an Odoo baseline", and `docs/reads-over-post.md`'s ranking is superseded. Cost of learning this: **$0.0998**, one fresh learn; both replays and the census were free -- against a marking slice that would have touched the write rail. `benchmarks/mark_flip_probe.py` ships with the finding. **WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE**: why the locator fails. `th:nth-of-type(6)` with `anchor_id: null` is R3.7's overloaded-None shape, and whether this is generated-DOM ambiguity, a resolver gap, or the recorder capturing a weak anchor is unmeasured -- that is the next question for Odoo, and it is a different one from everything surveyed so far. **SUPERSEDED IN PART BY R4.115 (0.142.0) -- THE OBSERVATION STANDS, THE INTERPRETATION DOES NOT.** `bound_by: none` in both arms is real and re-measured; demotion still does not change the outcome. But the cause named here -- 'locator ambiguity on a generated DOM' -- is WRONG, and this finding's own sensor could not have seen it: the A/B compares two arms at ONE instant and never asks what was on the page. Measured since: on a RENDERED page the same spec binds uniquely on the first candidate (`bound_by: exact-text`, n=1 everywhere); at the failing call the page holds `thead th` 0 and 3 characters of body. The blocker is a READINESS RACE. The consequence for the plan is unchanged and now doubly held: R4.27 is still not the Odoo blocker, and 2.4b must not be costed as a marking fix -- but nor should it be costed as a locator fix.

findings.summary: **THE REPLAY READS PAGE STATE BEFORE A CLIENT-RENDERED APP HAS PAINTED IT, AND THAT -- NOT THE LOCATOR -- IS WHAT FAILS ON ODOO.** R4.114 measured `bound_by: none` in both arms of a mark-flip A/B and concluded locator ambiguity on a generated DOM. **The locator is fine.** On a RENDERED page the failing spec resolves uniquely on the FIRST candidate -- census over the live page: `exact-text` n=1, substring n=1, css n=1, and the real `resolve(unique=True)` returns BOUND with `sink={'bound_by': 'exact-text'}`. Tier 3 is doubly unavailable (`role='span'` is not in `KNOWN_ROLES`, and `len(anchor)==60 == _ANCHOR_MAX` so the truncation branch nulls the scope), and it does not matter, because Tier 1 binds outright. **WHAT THE REPLAY IS ACTUALLY LOOKING AT**, captured by wrapping `locators.resolve` during a real failing replay: `title='Odoo'`, `thead th` **0**, `exact_text` 0, `css_n` 0, **`body_chars` 3**. The page is a shell. `BrowserSession.goto` waits only for `domcontentloaded` and `flow.py` resolves immediately; the settle curve says blank at 0.31 s and BOUND at 0.70 s, twice. **THREE SITES, all reached with no settle**: (1) `resolve(page, step.locator, unique=True)` -> 'locator unresolved or ambiguous'; (2) the gate's `scope_fingerprint(target)` -> 'form/section drift' -- traced at a real gate call, t+0ms reads `d326be1294743f5f` which is the PREVIOUS step's recorded scope and t+100ms reads `7b7d0c62763dd625` which is exactly this step's, so the gate is not seeing drift, it is seeing the past; (3) the gate's whole-page `session.snapshot()` -> 'page drift'. **THE SUBSTRATE CONTRAST IS TOTAL AND MEASURED**: Gitea 7/7 complete at domcontentloaded (143/117/175 elements, settled count identical) with ONE whole-page fingerprint each; Odoo **0/7**, every scenario exactly **5 elements and 1 character**, taking 3-4 distinct fingerprints and settling at 0.62-1.08 s. The 5 is R4.93's independently measured Odoo skeleton, from a different slice. **THE MECHANISM IS NOT LLM LATENCY** -- a first draft said the learn is protected by the model round-trip and that is WRONG in its ordering: `flow.py`'s author loop is `snapshot() -> decide() -> act()`, so the learn's FIRST observation is taken at the same point in wall time as the replay's first resolve and sees the same skeleton (R4.40 measured it at 5). What rescues the learn is that the loop **RE-OBSERVES every turn**, so a turn spent on a skeleton is recoverable; the replay resolves ONCE per step and `mode='replay'` nulls the provider, so `_maybe_heal` returns immediately and one miss is terminal. That is a cheaper and stronger statement: **a guard on a sibling path never applied to the mechanism**, which is CLAUDE.md's own named predictor.
